On Uncle Abu Salim's door hung a lantern of copper and glass. He hung it up every evening, and it lit the whole alley right to the end.

The neighbourhood children played in its light after Maghrib, and Abu Salim never put it out until they had all gone home.

One evening Yazan was playing ball alone in the alley. He kicked it hard, and it flew up and hit the lantern. The glass shattered, and the light went out.

Yazan stood frozen in the dark. No one came out, and no one had seen him. So he grabbed his ball and hurried into his house.

In the morning Abu Salim stood at his door looking at the broken glass, and the neighbours gathered around him.

One of them said, "I saw Rami playing ball here yesterday." Rami was a boy whose family had just moved into the neighbourhood, and people did not know him yet.

Rami's mother came to apologise for her son, with Rami behind her saying, "I didn't do anything!" — but no one believed him.

Yazan was standing with the others, hearing and seeing everything. His heart was pounding, but his tongue would not move.

The day dragged on. Whenever Yazan saw Rami sitting alone on a stone at the edge of the neighbourhood, he looked at the ground and walked on.

When night came, he could not sleep. From his window he could see the alley lying dark — and he had never seen it dark before that night.

Early in the morning he got up, broke open his money box, gathered what was inside into a handkerchief, and walked to Abu Salim's house, his legs feeling heavy.

He knocked on the door, and Abu Salim came out. Yazan held out the handkerchief and said, "I broke the lantern, Uncle — not Rami."

Abu Salim looked at him for a long time. Then he gave the handkerchief back and said, "Glass for a lantern can be bought for a few coins, Yazan. But what you have brought me now can't be bought."

Then he said, "But there's one more thing you still need to do."

Abu Salim walked with him to Rami, and in front of him and the neighbours Yazan said, "I'm the one who broke it. I kept quiet while you got the blame."

Rami was quiet for a moment, then said, "I never thought anyone would clear my name." And he held out his hand to Yazan and shook it.

Then the three of them sat by the door. Abu Salim took out the broken glass and brought new glass, while Yazan and Rami held the lantern until he had fixed it in place.

He showed them how to wind the wire around the glass to hold it firm. Whenever the wire slipped from their fingers, he handed it back to them with a smile, until they got it right.

When evening came, Abu Salim hung the lantern on his door, and it lit the alley just as before.

The neighbourhood children played in its light — and Yazan and Rami played on the same team.

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَكُونُوا مَعَ الصَّادِقِينَ﴾

📖 At-Tawbah 119. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.
